item.content:encoded:
That addendum kills it. Space does not work that way. You don't go up to some distance and then you're in orbit, you go sideways so that by the time you've fallen to the ground you've missed. You would need to be constantly firing downwards to cancel out the reversed gravity to not get pushed away. Furthermore, geostationary orbits are way, way, way higher than 80km.

Making it even worse, getting up to 80km is actually pretty easy with modern rocketry - heck, X-15 could (just barely, admittedly) do it back in the 1960s. Some of the containment procedures cost way more than a couple investigative flights would.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
We just had a heavy rainstorm here the other day, so I have a very fresh mental image of just how much stuff is laying around outside to get wet. When you consider that even a small raincloud could saturate several square miles, it is appalling how much mass this cloud must "eat" with every event.

Along with other practical questions already raised (i.e.: how does the rain know where one thing stops and another begins?), I think it's very vital to say that the anomaly does not affect gases or other liquids. Because if it did, the local depressurization of the atmosphere would create such hellacious windstorms that there would be no chance of any survivors.

item.content:encoded:
It's perfectly fair to decide you don't like the article, but there is a far more than "arbitrary" differentiation between objects and other objects. Even identical metals have a layer of oxidization preventing the two items from spot-welding. Other items are held together by molecular bonds or physically woven together, or held by epoxies.

That said, I don't disagree that the manner in which affected materials are altered could use some explanation. The point that it's just abritrarily magical is a bit out there, and I ought to figure that out. Maybe it only affects non-permeable substances. Maybe it only works while the liquid is in contact with the object. I should define that, and I'll get to it when I get home tonight.

I'm sorry the story fell flat for you, man. :( I get caught between elaborating and losing the reader in word vomit, or trying to keep it minimal and losing some people who WANT a full-blown tale. I can't really make everyone happy, much as I'd like to, but I'll look at it and see if I can refine it to drive everything home more effectively.

item.content:encoded:
I don't like this.

The primary effect here is pants-shittingly terrifying to me, and this doesn't do anything good with it in my opinion. From the start of the encounter summary and to the end I was just bored; the story here does nothing to me.

In addition, that part about the entirety of the object being immediately affected from any contact with the affected water just flat-out murders all of my suspension of disbelief. This is extreme levels of magical hand-waiving. There is no fundamental separation between one objects and others, it's all arbitrary. There is no reason why the border between the skin and other tissues is ignored, while the border between clothes and the skin is sacred; or why tires aren't considered to be a part of a car, or passengers aren't considered to be a part of the plane.

item.content:encoded:
I can't please everyone. Originally, the logs were more clinical and had less intended emotional impact, but that was disappointing to some folks, too.

The actual skip is 80km above the earth's surface. Top plane ceiling was Helios, a NASA plane that managed 90k FEET. To hit 80k METERS requires a shuttle, or at least a rocket to send instruments into the cloud. That's an insane amount of money thrown away. Tornadoes happen. This is easily explained as a tornado. It's not containable and needs no protection, so keeping knowledge of its existence secure from the public is all that the Foundation is really interested in doing.

Still… hm. I'll add a bit about scheduling a satellite launch rocket to pass through the cloud, designed to avoid drifting into space instead of designed to avoid drifting towards the surface.

E: I've added details about the difficulty of reaching the SCP and pending proposals to do so, anyway. I'd like to note that the Foundation can't know much about this thing, because they can't get close to it. It's basically orbital. I may write a piece later describing the satellite launch or something.

item.content:encoded:
No. That's not how SCP-682 works. SCP-682 is not Mega Man. It does not gain the properties of things, just adapts its own properties to survive whatever is thrown at it.

682 would probably find some way to either tether itself to the ground until the effect wore off, or spontaneously attain negative mass to re-reverse the effects of gravity on it.

item.content:encoded:
This is really weird. I sort of have to assume this is how the cloud 'eats'; that bit about things vanishing when they hit the actual cloud seemed to be key. But is there really nothing we can do about this other than clean up after it and suppress knowledge of its existence? The encounter log talks about flying through the iridescent clouds, but what about flying into the skip itself? This isn't a "wouldn't it be cool if", but more that I feel the Foundation's reaction to the thing is "Oh well, what can ya do?"

That said, I didn't think the log was all that great. Tone seems to get worse as it goes. I don't particularly care about Captain Finch. (And if you're going to redact his first initial, why not just leave his name out entirely and refer to him as "the captain"?) I'd rather know something about this thing's habits. How often does it 'infect' other clouds? Does it move in a particular pattern? Does it appear to hunt, or is it just anti-grav'ing things at random? Downvote for now.
